info.bio:
Pete Seeger (Nueva York, 1919),es junto con Woody Guthrie y Leadbelly  el músico más importante de folk norteamericano del siglo XX.

Siempre vinculado al comunismo y a los movimientos revolucionarios, llegó a estar en la lista negra del siniestro senador Mc Carthy durante la caza de brujas a comienzos de los 50.

Formó el grupo the almanac singers junto a Guthrie y ha sido de maestro y referente de artistas tan importantes como Joan Baez, Bob Dylan o Bruce Springsteen, que en 06 sacó un album entero con canciones de Pete Seeger.

scenes.name: Rock'n'roll
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fusión de rhythm'n'blues y country, con mucho más peso del primero. Chuck Berry inventa en 1955 el rock'n'roll tal como se conocerá durante cincuenta años (la guitarra como instrumento protagonista, canciones propias que hablan a los adolescentes); Bo Diddley aporta el ritmo «hambone», Little Richard y Esquerita el histerismo y el maquillaje (el primer «decadence-rock»), Jerry Lee Lewis el piano feroz y Sun Records el rockabilly. Elvis Presley es, para Scaruffi, «la primera gran estafa del rock'n'roll». Buddy Holly y Eddie Cochran abren otra vía; en paralelo nacen el soul (Ray Charles), la exótica (Martin Denny, Esquivel), la música electrónica de cinta y, en Gran Bretaña, el skiffle.

scenes.name: Folk revival y canción protesta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El acontecimiento más importante del cambio de década: el folk revival (Kingston Trio, festival de Newport) convierte la música en algo más que entretenimiento. Con «Blowing In The Wind» de Dylan, la canción protesta se vuelve el paradigma del Greenwich Village y el folk-singer muta en cantautor. Otros buscan la innovación: Davy Graham, Sandy Bull (fusión de folk, blues, jazz y raga) y John Fahey, que inventa el «American primitivism».

podcast.title: Activism and Friendships
podcast.body: Seeger was friends with both Woody Guthrie and Lead Belly in the 1940s and dedicated his later career to the same kind of left-wing activism that Guthrie had pursued. "He had been friends with both Woody Guthrie and Lead Belly in the 40s, and he dedicated his later career to the same kind of left-wing activism the Guthrie had taken part in."

podcast.title: Blacklisting as Solo Artist
podcast.body: As a result of his refusal to testify, Seeger, along with The Weavers, was blacklisted from radio and TV as a solo artist. "As a result, the Weevers were blacklisted from Radio and TV, as was Seeger as a solo artist."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 92: "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" by the Tokens

podcast.title: Central Figure in New York Folk Scene
podcast.body: Seeger was a key figure in a group of left-wing intellectuals and folk singers in New York, which included Alan Lomax and Lead Belly, centered at Armanac House in Greenwich Village. This environment spawned The Armanac Singers and The Weavers. "he hooked up with a group of left-wing intellectuals and folk singers, centering on Alan Lomax, Pete Seeger, and Leab Belly."

podcast.title: Efforts to Compensate Solomon Linda
podcast.body: Upon discovering that Solomon Linda, not tradition, was the author of "In Boube," Seeger insisted that all future money he would have made from "Wimoweh" go to Linda and sent Linda a check for a thousand dollars for money already earned. However, his assumption that his colleagues would honor the agreement proved false, and Linda received nothing from them. "As it turned out, he didn't. When he discovered that Solomon Linda had written the song, that it wasn't just a traditional song, he insisted that all future money he would have made from it go to Linda, and sent Linda a check for a thousand dollars for the money he'd already earned."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Elder Statesman of Folk Scene
podcast.body: Pete Seeger was regarded as the "elder statesman" of the Greenwich Village folk scene, around whom the "Stalinist" faction of folkies coalesced. "There were the Stalinists, who had coalesced around Pete Seagher, the elder statesman of the scene"

podcast.title: Frugal Life and Philanthropy
podcast.body: Seeger was known for not caring much about money, donating the vast majority of his earnings to worthy causes and living frugally. "But Seeger was someone who didn't care much about money at all. He donated the vast majority of his money to worthy causes, and lived frugally."

podcast.title: Important Figure in Folk Music Revival
podcast.body: Pete Seeger is described as a hugely important figure in the history of the folk music rebirth of the 1960s. "Pete Seeger, the most important member of The Weavers, is a figure who is hugely important in the history of the folk music rebirth of the 1960s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Labeled as Communist (1930s-1940s)
podcast.body: Pete Seeger, along with Woody Guthrie, used folk music in the 1930s and 1940s to spread messages that resulted in both of them being labeled as communists. His membership in the American Communist Party later caused him significant difficulties. "Seeger was a member of the American Communist Party, and that's something that caused him all sorts of headaches later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Philosophical Disagreement
podcast.body: Seeger's camp believed that a song's quality was secondary to its potential for social good, a view that conflicted with the blues and ballad singers who prioritized music itself. "Seagher's camp though that the quality of a song was secondary to the social good it could do, while the blues and ballad singers held at the important thing with the music, and any political or social good was a nice byproduct."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Privileged Background and Socialist Principles
podcast.body: Unlike many of his contemporary white folk singers, Seeger came from an incredibly privileged background, having attended Harvard as a classmate of John F. Kennedy. Despite this, he held very strong socialist principles. "Like most of the white folk singers of the period, he had an incredibly privileged background. He had attended Harvard as a classmate of John F. Kennedy."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 92: "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" by the Tokens

podcast.title: Quit The Weavers Over Tobacco Commercial
podcast.body: Driven by his strong principles against tobacco and advertising, Seeger quit The Weavers when they accepted an offer to do a commercial for tobacco. Despite his disapproval, he honored a prior commitment and appeared in the commercial. "But Seeger didn't approve of tobacco or advertising, and quit the group because of it. Though, because he'd made a commitment to the group, he did appear on the commercial, not wanting to break his word."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 92: "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" by the Tokens

podcast.title: Refusal to Testify to HUAC
podcast.body: Called before the House on American Activities Committee as a past Communist Party member, Seeger took the risky option of refusing to testify on First Amendment grounds. He asserted that his political activities, voting history, and party membership were his private business, spending much of the next decade under threat of prison. "But Seeger took the riskier option of simply refusing on first amendment grounds. He said, quite rightly, that his political activities, voting history, and party membership were nobody's business except his, and he wasn't going to testify about them in front of Congress."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 92: "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" by the Tokens

podcast.title: Second Payment to Linda's Daughters
podcast.body: Just before Ryan Mulan's article exposed the disparity in royalties, Seeger received a $6,000 payment when a commercial used "Wimoweh." Realizing he had been receiving royalties for "Wimoweh" all along, despite his earlier instructions, he calculated his total earnings from the song, which amounted to $12,000, and sent a check for that sum to Linda's daughters. "Pete T. Gennotis to $6,000 payment, which came to him when a commercial used Wimmerway, rather than The Lion sleeps tonight."

xref.title: Challenged the Status Quo
xref.body: Bob Dylan emerged in the wake of the folk movement pioneered by Woody Guthrie and Pete Seeger. He was notable for his willingness to directly challenge and critique the prevailing social and political conditions of his time. "The folk movement that came in their wake gave us people like Bob Dylan, who had no trouble poking the status quo in the eye."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
